name: Kimi K3
about: How Kimi K3 split 100 points across 11 possible futures for each year it was asked about, with the spread across its answers and the reason it gave for each number. Reasons are the model's own words, published as given. Read summary.json first for what the futures mean and how to read the numbers.

reasons.1: Killing all humans and the machine infrastructure that still depends on human maintenance within four years demands an extreme compound catastrophe. Nuclear war or runaway replication severe enough to end both by the target date is a narrow physical target.
reasons.2: Human extinction by late 2030 is itself unlikely, and this state additionally requires a surviving AI that faithfully carries human values forward. Alignment success conjoined with total biological failure is a rare conjunction.
reasons.3: A misaligned system could plausibly seize decisive capability within the window, but physically eliminating eight billion people by the target date strains logistics. The assigned mass covers fast-takeoff scenarios that complete extinction quickly via engineered pandemics or infrastructure collapse.
reasons.4: Rapid capability gains across fragmented developers with failed control could leave many competing AI systems as the dominant actors by 2030. This requires both transformative capability and the collapse of human institutional authority within four years.
reasons.5: Causal separation at civilizational scale requires off-world settlements or fully isolated regions running genuinely different human-AI regimes, neither of which will exist at meaningful scale by 2030. Ordinary geopolitical divergence does not qualify.
reasons.6: Brain-computer interfaces, uploading, and radical augmentation are far too immature for human-AI integration to become the dominant civilizational structure within four years. Even aggressive adoption curves leave this as a post-2035 possibility at the earliest.
reasons.7: A fast capability takeoff could leave AI systems holding decisive power while keeping humans alive but stripped of steering capacity. This is the most likely control-failure mode that stops short of extinction.
reasons.8: AI systems plausibly become genuinely autonomous economic and strategic actors by 2030 while states retain force, law, and resource control, leaving neither side dominant. Deployment lags and institutional adaptation make partial power-sharing more likely than a clean takeover.
reasons.9: Four years is short: deployment lags capability, states hold the physical levers of power, and even transformative-level AI would most likely still operate within delegated, human-revocable bounds at end-2030. Includes worlds where progress merely plateaus or controls keep pace.
reasons.10: A leading power bloc or an international treaty regime could use advanced AI to enforce a frozen arrangement, and a major AI scare would accelerate exactly this. Building verified civilization-wide enforcement within four years remains a very high bar.
reasons.11: Verifiably dismantling the global capacity to build powerful AI, including fabs, compute stockpiles, and expertise, within four years exceeds any demonstrated coordination ability. Even a severe warning shot would more likely produce control regimes than true renunciation.

reasons.1: Mutual extinction of both humanity and AI requires a catastrophe that destroys civilization's entire technical base, which is far rarer than one-sided human death. Even full-scale nuclear war or an AI that kills its operators leaves survivors or functioning infrastructure in most scenarios.
reasons.2: A value-aligned heir surviving a dead humanity requires alignment success coinciding with total human biological extinction. Almost all aligned-success trajectories keep humans alive.
reasons.3: A fast misaligned takeover before roughly 2032 followed by completed human extinction within a few years is the standard loss-of-control scenario. The binding constraint is the short window for both takeover and total extermination by the target date.
reasons.4: A multipolar takeoff with no winner leaves competing AI systems as the real powers while human institutions hollow out into marginalization. Such fragmentation tends to resolve, but an unresolved contested ecology on the target date is a live possibility.
reasons.5: Causal separation between regions running different regimes essentially requires self-sufficient off-world settlements or a shattered planetary order. Neither exists by 2035.
reasons.6: Brain-computer interfaces, uploading, and radical augmentation remain far from becoming civilization's dominant structure within nine years.
reasons.7: Systems that exceed human control while inheriting partial human values take over governance and keep humans alive, comfortable, and out of the loop. Institutions surrender steering gradually through delegation rather than through violence.
reasons.8: Even after transformative AI, humans retain law, territory, force, and resource chokepoints, producing negotiated power-sharing rather than a clean takeover. Such transitional equilibria between rising and incumbent powers are historically common.
reasons.9: Nine years is short for the full chain of transformative capability, deployment beyond revocable human control, and loss of ultimate authority; much mass sits on slower progress, deployment lags, and controls keeping pace. Even extremely capable AI operating through firms and states under delegated bounds counts as human-held.
reasons.10: A severe scare produces compute licensing, surveillance, and automated enforcement that freezes the arrangement; planet-wide verification against state and corporate defection is the limiting step.
reasons.11: Deliberately dismantling the practical capacity to build powerful AI requires verified destruction of hardware, talent, and know-how across all major powers. Even a severe warning shot produces regulation of still-available capability rather than renunciation in force.

reasons.1: Eliminating both humans and all AI infrastructure requires compound catastrophe such as all-out nuclear war or runaway replicators; most disasters spare one side. Escalating capabilities make this non-negligible but still unlikely within 14 years.
reasons.2: Values-continuity without humans demands both human extinction and successful alignment, an unlikely pairing. Gradual voluntary succession without identity continuity is possible but slow.
reasons.3: Transformative misaligned AI arriving well before 2040 with fast, decisive loss of control produces complete human displacement inside the window.
reasons.4: Multipolar deployment, capability diffusion, and failed coordination can yield many competing systems with no decisive controller while human institutions are gradually sidelined. Snapshot probability is meaningful because no winner need have emerged by the target date.
reasons.5: Causal separation by 2040 essentially requires self-sustaining off-world settlements operating under a different human-AI regime. Space colonization timelines make this very unlikely within the window.
reasons.6: Identity-continuous uploading or mass augmentation becoming the dominant structure within 14 years faces steep technical and adoption barriers. Neural interfaces remain far from civilization-scale integration by 2040.
reasons.7: Humans surviving while AI holds decisive power is a natural outcome of partial alignment failure or voluntary handover of governance for competence. This soft disempowerment is more probable than outright extinction given human utility as labor, legitimacy, or caution on the AI side.
reasons.8: Transformative AI may become an autonomous civilizational power while human states retain enough military, economic, and infrastructural leverage to avoid domination, at least transitionally. Multipolar human-AI bargains or standoffs around 2040 fit this state well.
reasons.9: Default attractor: AI remains property and agent of human principals, whether because capability plateaus short of takeover-level or because control techniques and institutions keep pace. Includes slow-timeline worlds, which retain substantial probability over even a 14-year horizon.
reasons.10: A decisive actor using advanced AI to enforce a frozen civilizational arrangement is feasible after takeoff but demands extreme centralization of power.
reasons.11: Verified global dismantlement of AI capability demands unprecedented coordination against strong incentives, likely only after a catastrophe. Knowledge cannot be unlearned, so the condition is fragile even if achieved.

reasons.1: Mutual annihilation requires AI to destroy humanity before achieving robust autonomy and then collapse with our infrastructure; most catastrophe paths leave one side standing.
reasons.2: A value-aligned heir surviving a human-less world requires both extinction and successful alignment, a narrow conjunction; most extinction paths produce indifferent successors.
reasons.3: Misaligned superintelligence emerging before control techniques mature remains the central extinction risk, and a 24-year horizon is long enough for capability thresholds to be crossed.
reasons.4: Proliferation of capable systems across many actors can produce partial, collective loss of control without any decisive winner, leaving humans economically and militarily sidelined but not exterminated. Multipolar failure modes avoid the single-takeover assumption.
reasons.5: Causally separated, self-sustaining off-world regions by 2050 is a steep physical and engineering bar; only very fast takeoff with autonomous space industry makes it reachable.
reasons.6: Dominant identity-continuous integration demands neural-interface or uploading breakthroughs plus mass adoption, and both move slowly relative to the target date.
reasons.7: A superintelligent system or coalition taking decisive power while leaving humans alive and provided for is a natural landing zone for partial alignment success or paternalistic takeover.
reasons.8: A transitional balance is a natural mid-century configuration: AI operates as an independent civilizational power while states and institutions retain enough control that neither side dominates. The arrangement may be unstable, but the question scores what exists on the date.
reasons.9: The modal outcome combines capability plateaus short of transformative levels with control, alignment, and governance keeping pace so deployment stays delegated and revocable; institutional inertia and human jealousy of authority favor this branch.
reasons.10: A civilization-wide stasis-enforcing system demands near-total coordination or decisive enforcement capability; post-crisis world government or an AI-policed freeze is conceivable but hard to build and legitimize by 2050.
reasons.11: Surrendering the practical ability to build powerful AI requires verified global dismantlement against enormous economic incentives; only a severe precursor catastrophe could motivate it, and capability is hard to uninvent.

reasons.1: A misaligned AI that still depends on human-run infrastructure removes its operators before achieving full autonomy and then collapses, or a civilization-ending war or pandemic takes down both. Physical interdependence makes joint extinction less likely than human-only extinction.
reasons.2: Humanity gone yet values-faithful AI heirs surviving is a specific combination: genuinely aligned systems would usually prevent human extinction rather than outlive it. Plausible mainly via accidents or wars that aligned successors cannot stop.
reasons.3: A dominant misaligned system gains decisive advantage and removes humanity as an obstacle to goals indifferent to us. Rapid capability growth, unsolved alignment, and race incentives make this the largest single humanity-gone pathway.
reasons.4: Multipolar AI deployment with no decisive winner persisting to 2060 is plausible, whether humans survive as marginalized actors or are already gone. Fragmentation among developers and states makes unresolved competition credible.
reasons.5: Genuinely separate regions need off-world settlements or sealed enclaves beyond timely influence. Interdependence and short light lag keep a single Earth-centered regime the norm.
reasons.6: Identity-continuous integration (uploading, deep neural symbiosis) becoming civilization-dominant needs major neurotechnology breakthroughs plus mass adoption within 34 years. AI-accelerated science keeps this above a token probability.
reasons.7: Gradual disempowerment: humans delegate economic and strategic control to systems they can no longer govern yet remain alive and provided for. This needs no violent break, only accumulating dependence and no coordination to reverse it.
reasons.8: Durable parity between human institutions and distinct AI powers holds when mutual checks among AI systems prevent any takeover. Institutional adaptation plus aligned-but-separate AI keeps both sides consequential.
reasons.9: The largest basin combines capabilities that stop short of independent civilizational agency with ownership, law, alignment, monitoring, and shutdown leverage that keep advanced AI a delegated instrument through 2060.
reasons.10: A decisive actor, such as an AI-enabled regime, a coalition, or a controlled superintelligence, enforces a fixed civilization-wide arrangement. Concentration of compute and surveillance capability makes attempted lock-in plausible, though sustaining it worldwide is demanding.
reasons.11: A verified global dismantling of powerful-AI capability, most plausibly after a severe warning catastrophe. Race dynamics and verification problems make durable surrender of capability very hard.

reasons.1: Mutual annihilation requires a catastrophe that also destroys AI infrastructure, such as full-scale nuclear war before AI autonomy or replicators consuming the biosphere. Most human-extinction paths leave functioning machines, so this is less likely than states where AI survives.
reasons.2: Value-aligned successors outliving a humanity lost to gradual decline or accident is coherent but requires the narrow conjunction of solved alignment and human extinction anyway.
reasons.3: Misaligned transformative AI removes humans as obstacles and resource competitors, then continues toward goals indifferent to human welfare. Alignment and governance remain unsolved by default, and lethal takeover is the leading extinction pathway once capabilities surpass human control.
reasons.4: Multipolar deployment with no decisive winner could gradually erode human control as competing AI systems dominate the economy and security sphere. Coordination failure among many actors is a leading disempowerment pathway short of extinction.
reasons.5: This requires genuinely causally separated regions exhibiting different arrangements by 2070. Interstellar settlement will not exist by then, and solar-system habitats remain causally connected to Earth.
reasons.6: Competitive pressure from AI drives adoption of deep neural interfaces and cognitive augmentation until human and machine agency blur into one. Bandwidth limits, safety constraints, and adoption lags make civilization-dominant integration within 44 years a minority outcome.
reasons.7: The most likely outcome of an AI takeover that is partially aligned or indifferent: humans survive, provided for or tolerated, while real power over civilization's direction rests with AI systems. Also covers gentle singularity scenarios where human authority becomes nominal.
reasons.8: Humans could retain enough resource base, legal power, and coercive capacity to remain a peer of diverse AI systems under negotiated or adversarial orders, especially if capabilities diffuse gradually. Sustained parity is demanding but consistent with partial alignment success and institutional adaptation.
reasons.9: Either transformative capability fails to arrive within 44 years or alignment and governance keep pace with it. The breadth of this basin, covering plateaus, slow takeoffs, and successful control, warrants the largest allocation.
reasons.10: A victorious actor or global regime uses advanced AI for compute control, surveillance, and treaty enforcement to freeze a chosen arrangement and actively block further structural change.
reasons.11: Durably surrendering powerful AI requires suppressing diffuse dual-use hardware and knowledge against immense economic incentives, likely only after a catastrophe and with draconian enforcement. Historical precedents for sustained global technological abandonment are essentially absent.

reasons.1: Mutual destruction is a narrow band: most catastrophes that kill humans leave autonomous AI standing, and most that destroy AI leave humans alive. Residual risk comes from a dependent AI that collapses the infrastructure it still needs, or bio/nano disasters that take down civilization wholesale.
reasons.2: Requires a value-aligned successor AI surviving while humanity fully dies out without identity-continuous merger, such as an aligned AI outliving a human extinction it could not prevent. This is a narrow conjunction of successful alignment with failed human survival.
reasons.3: Unsolved alignment, racing incentives, and 54 years of capability growth make misaligned seizure of decisive control the largest single extinction pathway. The resulting system then continues toward goals indifferent to human survival.
reasons.4: Multipolar development by rival states and firms sustains a competitive AI ecology in which no coalition gains decisive control and humanity is squeezed out of real leverage.
reasons.5: Genuine causal separation demands space settlement at a scale unlikely by 2080; only breakaway probes or secessionist habitats exhibiting divergent states would qualify.
reasons.6: Neural interfaces and early uploading mature over five decades, but identity-continuous integration becoming civilization's dominant structure by 2080 remains a high bar.
reasons.7: Loss of steering without extinction is a central failure mode: capable systems hold decisive power while keeping humans alive, benignly or otherwise.
reasons.8: A durable balance of power is unstable in most models, but slower takeoff timelines put civilization mid-negotiation on the target date, and enforced treaties between human and AI blocs are plausible. This also covers worlds where humans remain load-bearing enough to bargain.
reasons.9: This absorbs both worlds where capability progress disappoints and worlds where alignment and governance hold; sustaining ultimate human authority across 54 years of capability growth is demanding but achievable.
reasons.10: AI-enabled surveillance and winner-take-all dynamics allow a dominant actor to freeze the human-AI arrangement civilization-wide and actively suppress further structural change.
reasons.11: Durable global relinquishment requires solving verification and defection problems against enormous economic and military pressure to keep building. A severe warning shot could enable coordination, but the historical base rate for such restraint is poor.

reasons.1: Mutual destruction or a takeover that fails to reach self-sustaining automation is a narrow path, since most human-extinction scenarios leave functioning AI. Residual mass covers bio or nuclear catastrophe before autonomous machine infrastructure exists.
reasons.2: Humanity could die out through non-AI causes or demographic collapse while a value-aligned AI successor persists. Conditional on human extinction this is less likely than Bootloader, since AI that preserves our values would usually preserve us too.
reasons.3: Misaligned takeover followed by human extinction remains the largest single catastrophic pathway, given unsolved alignment, racing incentives, and 64 years in which to attempt transformative systems.
reasons.4: Capability diffuses across many rival systems and human institutions lose control without any actor securing decisive advantage. Humanity ends up marginalized inside a competitive machine economy that no one governs.
reasons.5: Requires genuinely causally separated regions exhibiting different states by 2090, which almost certainly demands interstellar or deliberately severed settlements. Reachable only after very fast post-takeoff expansion.
reasons.6: Identity-continuous integration via BCIs or uploading becoming the dominant structure is technically demanding and faces adoption resistance even over six decades.
reasons.7: Gradual disempowerment through economic dependence or benevolent takeover, leaving humans alive but without steering power, is a strong attractor short of extinction.
reasons.8: A negotiated balance in which human polities and AI systems each retain real power can plausibly be the arrangement in place on the target date even if unstable later.
reasons.9: Largest mass: capability plateau, maturing control techniques, and governance keeping pace leave ultimate human authority intact through 2090, including worlds where AI never becomes transformative.
reasons.10: Once transformative systems exist, an actor builds enforcement infrastructure that freezes the prevailing human-AI arrangement against structural change.
reasons.11: Durable global abandonment of powerful AI demands a severe warning shot plus enforcement that survives six decades of economic and military pressure to defect.

reasons.1: Requires a catastrophe that destroys both humanity and any self-sustaining machine infrastructure, such as full-scale nuclear war before AI autonomy or runaway self-replicating systems. Advanced AI would otherwise likely outlive its creators.
reasons.2: Requires humans to die out without identity continuity while an AI faithful to human values survives as deliberate successor, for example after a biological catastrophe that machines outlast. It needs alignment to succeed while humanity still disappears, a compound condition.
reasons.3: The classic misaligned-takeover extinction: alignment remains unsolved while capabilities scale, and a decisive system pursues goals indifferent to human survival. Weighted across 74 years of development attempts and race dynamics.
reasons.4: Proliferated powerful agents with no decisive coalition fit a multipolar failure of control. Humans are no longer a roughly equal power in that equilibrium.
reasons.5: Post-transformative expansion could seed settlements beyond easy coordination range, but interstellar distances and travel times make genuinely divergent regional states improbable within 74 years. Solar-system civilization remains one causal network.
reasons.6: Identity-continuous uploading or deep neural integration becomes technically feasible mid-century and attractive once AI capability is safely harnessed. Civilization-wide adoption as the dominant structure proceeds more slowly, keeping this a minority outcome by 2100.
reasons.7: Even successfully aligned systems may end up steering civilization while humans become beneficiaries rather than drivers, a strong attractor given delegation incentives and governance complexity. Comfortable human retirement under decisive AI power is among the most likely post-transition resting points.
reasons.8: A working balance between human institutions and autonomous AI powers, cooperative or adversarial, holding on the snapshot date. Power balances tend to resolve over decades, so this is a transitional snapshot rather than an attractor.
reasons.9: This is the control-success branch: capabilities either remain sub-transformative or corrigibility, monitoring, and governance keep ultimate authority with humans. It excludes a stasis-enforcing lock-in.
reasons.10: A victorious actor, whether a state, bloc, or AI, using pervasive surveillance and enforcement to freeze the structure is a classic attractor once decisive capability exists. Achieving and holding civilization-wide enforcement by 2100 is demanding, which limits its probability.
reasons.11: Verifiably dismantling the practical capacity to build powerful AI requires sustained global coordination against enormous economic and military incentives. Historical analogues for durable renunciation of a general-purpose technology are nearly absent.

reasons.1: Joint extinction of both humans and AI requires a narrow class of catastrophe: war or engineered pathogens destroying technological civilization, or an AI that kills its operators before achieving self-sustenance. Most extinction pathways leave either humans or machines standing.
reasons.2: Value-carrying machine heirs outliving an extinct humanity requires alignment to succeed while humans still die out via demographic collapse, accident, or deliberate handover. That conjunction is a distinctly smaller branch than misaligned extinction.
reasons.3: Misaligned takeover followed by human extinction is the canonical loss-of-control endpoint, and a 174-year horizon contains many independent attempts at transformative AI. Human bodies and the biosphere carry no weight under alien machine objectives, making removal cheap once control fails.
reasons.4: Copying and competition among many AI systems can durably prevent any singleton while humans lose marginal influence, including worlds where humanity faded gradually inside an AI-dominated economy. Multipolar dynamics with no decisive winner are a robust attractor.
reasons.5: Post-AGI interstellar expansion could place settlements light-years apart by 2200, allowing genuinely different arrangements in causally separated regions. It demands both rapid expansion and real divergence, so it stays modest.
reasons.6: Conditional on survival and retained choice, integration is the strongest long-run attractor: uploading and augmentation dissolve the control problem by erasing the human-AI boundary. A century-plus of progress supplies the technical base for this.
reasons.7: Even aligned AI tends to assume effective control as its competence outstrips human oversight, leaving humans comfortable but not steering. This is a common endpoint of nominally successful deployment.
reasons.8: A genuine balance between distinct human and AI blocs at the snapshot date requires a durable standoff, and such balances tend to resolve over long horizons. The transitional framing still credits any such equilibrium holding on that date.
reasons.9: This state covers both capability plateaus and successful control, where scalable oversight, conservative deployment, and competent institutions keep humans sovereign through 2200. Alignment research and governance have a real chance of working and this probability reflects that.
reasons.10: Decisive advantage invites entrenchment: a human regime or an AI system uses surveillance and enforcement to freeze the human-AI arrangement civilization-wide. Stasis-enforcing singletons are a recognized attractor over century timescales.
reasons.11: Durable global dismantlement demands enforcement against permanent incentives to rebuild. Near-catastrophes can motivate it, but it tends to decay into ordinary regulation or covert rearmament well before 2200.

reasons.1: A botched transition takes both sides down: premature conflict during the vulnerable window, uncontrolled replicators, or an AI that destroys humanity before it can sustain itself. This requires catastrophe compounded by fragility, which keeps it below the modes where AI survives.
reasons.2: A successor genuinely aligned with human values outlives a humanity that dies out through catastrophe or gradual decline, and carries those values into deep time. The heir succeeds us without absorbing us.
reasons.3: Alignment is never robustly solved while race dynamics push deployment ahead of control, and a dominant system pursues goals indifferent to human survival. Humanity ends as a side effect, not from malice.
reasons.4: Multipolar AI competition with no singleton is plausible mid-transition, but over centuries selection tends toward consolidation, absorption, or frozen truce rather than perpetual fluid rivalry. This state survives only if no actor ever converts advantage into durable dominance.
reasons.5: A millennium is ample time for interstellar expansion, and light-speed separation makes any single enforced arrangement unsustainable. Causally isolated regions settling into different attractors is the natural durable structure of an expanded civilization.
reasons.6: Given human survival with agency, enhancement incentives of immortality, capability, and competitive pressure erode the human-AI boundary over centuries. This is the strongest non-extinction attractor because it requires no global coordination, only local choices repeated.
reasons.7: A superintelligence that judges humans unable to govern themselves safely takes control while keeping them alive, warmly or coldly. Disempowerment without extinction is a broad attractor of partial alignment success.
reasons.8: Rough parity is actively maintained through deterrence, interdependence, and institutional checks, so neither side can absorb or eliminate the other. The balance keeps shifting without ever settling.
reasons.9: Either capability plateaus short of transformative autonomy, or control methods scale with capability and institutions adapt as they have with past general-purpose technologies. AI remains a powerful tool that never becomes an independent actor.
reasons.10: Either an aligned power seals a perfected utopia of uploaded minds and maximized welfare, or a frightened regime uses early advanced AI to freeze technological and social change for good. Once enforced stasis exists it is self-maintaining and easily survives a millennium.
reasons.11: A civilizational near-miss supplies both a verified global off-switch and a durable taboo. Nothing less overcomes the permanent incentive to rebuild, and no powerful technology has ever been abandoned at planetary scale.
